doc.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022

chapter: Changes in the New York scene
title: Why she called it 'white'
summary: She says the music she loved was rooted in rhythm and blues by black players, while the newer approach came mostly from white male college graduates.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: If we — I hope you don’t mind me pursuing this because I like what you have to say about it, I think it’s important. If you call it Brooklyn white boy jazz —
Yeah, what is — why is it white?

Well when I came up, now this has changed also because now it’s not just white people that play like that. When I came up the people that I liked to listen to were basically black and they had their roots in rhythm, they cared about the rhythm and the blues was a part of it. You know the swing was a part of it, the blues was a part of it, and this shift was almost completely white. And now there are some other people of color, but the basic push in that direction was usually white male, college graduates. And so that’s why I called it that.
